title: Help these women (Philippians 4:1–3)
hook: Euodia and Syntyche, co-workers, are asked to agree

segments.voice: Yesterday, the runner's verse, and your line was press on. What was the one step you took forward instead of looking back? Day six hundred sixty-five.

Two names, and that's almost all we know. Euodia and Syntyche. Paul's letter is going to be read aloud to the whole church at Philippi, everyone in the room, and in the middle of it he names two women who aren't getting along. We don't know what the quarrel was about. Money, a meeting, a hurt word, a plan for the church. The letter never says, and it's honest to leave it there. What we do know is how Paul handles it. He doesn't take a side. He doesn't send a rebuke. He asks for help.

First he speaks to the whole church with real warmth: they are, in the King James Bible, "my joy and crown." Then: "I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord." Notice he says beseech twice, once to each woman. Neither gets named first as the problem. And same mind is a phrase he's used all through this letter: be likeminded, have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus. It doesn't mean agreeing on every detail. It means facing the same direction. Then he turns to someone else: "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel." Who is the yokefellow? Nobody knows. Some think it's a friend Paul doesn't name. Some think Yokefellow, Syzygos in Greek, was the man's actual name. Either way, a third person is asked to step in and help two people find their way back. And look how Paul describes these women. Not as troublemakers. As co-workers who labored with him in the gospel, side by side, along with Clement and the rest, "whose names are in the book of life." Their quarrel doesn't cancel their work. Philippi's church began, Acts says, with women at a place of prayer by a river, and Lydia opening her home. Women were there from the start. This week we've walked through Philippians: look to others, he emptied himself, shine like stars, two helpers honored, counting it loss, press on, and now two co-workers asked to agree.
screen: `CO-WORKERS, NAMES IN THE BOOK OF LIFE.`
then, large: `BE OF THE SAME MIND IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be the yokefellow. Settle, and breathe. Think of two people you know who have drifted apart or fallen out. Friends, siblings, coworkers, parents. Don't decide who's right. Paul didn't. Picture each of them, one and then the other, and remember one good thing each has done. Then ask yourself one question: is there a small way you could help, without taking sides? A shared invitation. A kind word about one to the other. Or simply not feeding the quarrel. If you pray, you can hold both of them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Syzygos. The Greek word for yokefellow, one who pulls in the same yoke, maybe even the man's own name: Paul's friend asked to help Euodia and Syntyche find the same mind again.
Your line: be of one mind. Today, when you hear one person complain about another, say something true and good about the one who isn't there. Day six hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Many churches ask a trusted third person, a pastor, elder or friend, to help members reconcile, and some read Philippians 4:2–3 when teaching about peacemaking in the congregation.

original.note: Greek: yokefellow, one who pulls in the same yoke. some think it was the man's actual name.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul scolding two women who were fighting.
what it means: Paul pleads with both co-workers equally and asks a third person to help them face the same way.
what a scholar hears: syzygos, yokefellow, may be a title or a proper name; and the Philippian church began with women at a place of prayer, according to Acts 16.

notes: The KJV spells the first name 'Euodias'; the Greek is Euodia (a woman's name). The script says Euodia in its own voice and quotes the KJV spelling.
Identity of the 'true yokefellow' (σύζυγε, vocative) is unknown; the proper-name reading is a minority but long-standing suggestion. Confirm.

Acts 16:13–15: women gathered at a place of prayer by the river; Lydia hosts Paul. Stated as Acts says.
